The One Big Beautiful Bill’s Medicaid “increase” is a classic D.C. shell game. The bill’s $1.6 trillion in proposed cuts fall $4.4 trillion short of pre-pandemic fiscal baselines, forcing states to absorb more costs while federal funding fails to keep pace with inflation and enrollment.

Section 3(b) allows bureaucratic reallocations that gut Medicaid’s purchasing power—calling that a 25% increase is like inflating a balloon with holes.

Real reform requires slashing pharma overpayments and consultant bloat, not creative accounting.
@RepFedorchak Then show us the text and where it says that.
@RepFedorchak Able bodied?

The CBO's nonpartisan analysis projects 7.8 million losing Medicaid under the One Big Beautiful Bill - far beyond the 4.8 million "able-bodied" figure being floated. This discrepancy stems from provisions like Section 44101's punitive work reporting mandates and Section 44122's retroactive coverage cuts from 3 months to 1. The bill's 1,000-page rushed structure creates bureaucratic tripwires that will boot low-income workers, disabled Americans, and caregivers from coverage even if technically eligible.

While the intent to streamline spending is valid, the execution fails basic accountability - it's like trying to fix a leaky faucet with a sledgehammer.

Real reform requires DOGE-style audits targeting $200B in annual Medicaid fraud by hospitals and pharma middlemen, not stripping coverage from vulnerable citizens caught in red tape.

The One Big Beautiful Bill’s $56.6B ag expansion proves Washington still thinks throwing cash solves problems. While raising crop insurance reference prices by 11-21% (Title I, Subtitle B) helps farmers navigate volatile markets, the bill also redirects $1.8B from conservation to bureaucratic pet projects.

Real reform? Letting producers operate without 30 million new base acres of red tape and ending the charade where “trade promotion” means doubling USDA’s global marketing budget to $285M/year.

North Dakota’s farmers don’t need D.C.’s “help” – they need Washington to stop looting their budgets to fund legacy programs like the Wool Apparel Manufacturing Trust Fund. Cut the bloat, keep the safety net.
@RepFedorchak Pass the issues separate.  You are all worthless.

The One Big Beautiful Bill’s farm provisions are a classic D.C. bait-and-switch. While reference price hikes and crop insurance updates sound good, the bill’s elimination of payment limits (Title I, Section 1001) turns subsidies into a slush fund for corporate agribusiness. CBO projections show 74% of payments flow to the top 10% of operations—many urban investors with zero dirt under their nails.

Instead of targeting real family farms drowning in input costs, this bloated package showers $56.6B on lobbyist-pushed loopholes while ignoring structural reforms. Rushed through reconciliation, it’s another trillion-dollar IOU for taxpayers.

Farm policy shouldn’t be a wealth transfer to the connected. Audit every line.
@RepFedorchak How about just pass a stand alone farm bill. This bill adds another 3 to 4 trillion to the deficit. That is NOT fiscal responsibility.

The One Big Beautiful Bill’s Medicaid work requirements are a long-overdue step to restore accountability. Cutting $930B in Medicaid bloat over a decade forces able-bodied adults to contribute—20hrs/week of work, volunteering, or training. Exemptions exist for parents, disabled, and veterans, but the core principle stands: taxpayer-funded benefits shouldn’t subsidize complacency.

D.C. bureaucrats hate it because it exposes their addiction to endless spending. Real reform means prioritizing those truly in need while slashing handouts to those who can work.

Medicaid’s purpose isn’t to fund couch potatoes—it’s a safety net, not a hammock.

Medicaid’s unsustainable growth proves the system is broken—not underfunded. The One Big Beautiful Bill slashes $1.6T in bloat while refocusing resources on core priorities: seniors, veterans, and vulnerable Americans. For too long, bureaucratic waste and non-citizen strain drained funds meant for citizens.

Reforms like mandatory work requirements and eligibility checks restore accountability. Critics crying “coverage loss” ignore the $55B annual fraud hemorrhage.

Real sustainability starts with cutting abuse, not writing blank checks. This bill forces Medicaid to serve Americans first—exactly as intended.
